manifest.sample:
<!-- Starter project file. Rename it and its assembly before you publish it.
     It builds as a library, so it compiles with no source files in it yet;
     add <OutputType>Exe</OutputType> when you write an entry point. -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>App</RootNamespace>
    <AssemblyName>App</AssemblyName>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

toolchain.why: Only the C# compiler runs flow-based nullable analysis and awaits/async checking; no analyzer package can see the null-state the compiler tracks, and only TreatWarningsAsErrors turns those CS-prefixed findings into a failing build.
toolchain.wiring: <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors> plus <Nullable>enable</Nullable> in a Directory.Build.props at the repository root, so every project inherits them without editing each csproj.

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line matching 'error CS8602: Dereference of a possibly null reference.'

toolchain.why: The Roslyn CA (code quality) and IDE (code style) analyzers catch design, security and dead-code defects the compiler ignores entirely - swallowed exceptions, SQL concatenation, insecure randomness, unread assignments.
toolchain.configSample:
root = true

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1031.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.CA1062.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2000.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2007.severity = none
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2016.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2100.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2200.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2201.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.CA5350.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.CA5351.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.CA5394.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0005.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0035.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0051.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0059.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0079.severity = warning
toolchain.wiring: <AnalysisLevel>latest-Recommended</AnalysisLevel> and <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild> in Directory.Build.props; IDE rules only run on command-line builds when EnforceCodeStyleInBuild is true.

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line matching 'error CA1031: Modify' naming the method that catches System.Exception

toolchain.why: Formatting drift is the noise that hides a real diff; dotnet format is the only tool here that can assert 'the tree is already canonical' without changing it, via --verify-no-changes.
toolchain.configSample:
root = true

[*.cs]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
charset = utf-8
csharp_new_line_before_open_brace = all
csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:warning
dotnet_sort_system_directives_first = true
dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0055.severity = warning

[*.{csproj,props,targets,runsettings}]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 2
toolchain.wiring: dotnet_diagnostic.IDE0055.severity = warning in .editorconfig, so the same formatting contract also fails the build under EnforceCodeStyleInBuild.

verify.expected: non-zero exit code and a list of files reported as needing formatting changes

toolchain.why: Only the xUnit analyzers understand test intent: they flag a skipped test, a public method that was never marked as a test, an unused Theory parameter and an unawaited async assertion - none of which the compiler or the CA rules see.
toolchain.configSample:
root = true

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit1004.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit1013.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit1026.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit1031.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit1049.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit2020.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.xUnit2021.severity = error
toolchain.wiring: <PackageReference Include="xunit.analyzers" /> in the test project (it also arrives transitively with the xunit metapackage), with the severities above pinned in .editorconfig.

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line matching 'error xUnit1004: Test methods should not be skipped'

toolchain.why: The only step that proves behaviour rather than shape; with TreatNoTestsAsError it is also the only step that can tell 'everything passed' apart from 'nothing ran'.
toolchain.wiring: <RunSettingsFilePath>$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory).runsettings</RunSettingsFilePath> in Directory.Build.props, so every test project picks the same settings up without a --settings flag.

verify.expected: exit code 1 with 'Failed!  - Failed:     1'; with TreatNoTestsAsError set to true a run that discovers zero tests also exits 1 instead of 0

toolchain.why: Restore-time audit is the only step that compares the resolved graph, including transitive packages, against the nuget.org vulnerability database; no analyzer reads package versions.

install.dotnet: dotnet nuget add source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json -n nuget.org

toolchain.wiring: <NuGetAuditMode>all</NuGetAuditMode> plus NU1901-NU1904 listed in <WarningsAsErrors>, so a vulnerable transitive package fails restore rather than printing a warning nobody reads.

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line matching 'error NU1903: Package ... has a known high severity vulnerability'

toolchain.why: Carries three checks nothing else in this ecosystem has: S2699 fails a test that contains no assertion at all, S108 fails any empty nested block, and S125 flags commented-out code - catching the 'make it green' shapes the CA rules miss.
toolchain.configSample:
root = true

[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.S108.severity = error
dotnet_diagnostic.S125.severity = warning
dotnet_diagnostic.S2699.severity = error
toolchain.wiring: <PackageReference Include="SonarAnalyzer.CSharp" PrivateAssets="all" /> in Directory.Build.props so it applies to every project, with the three severities pinned in .editorconfig. S125 is pinned at warning rather than error because SonarSource's own tracker documents false positives in its commented-out-code heuristic.

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line matching 'error S2699: Add at least one assertion to this test case.'

classes.title: Test skipped instead of fixed
agentModes: a session cannot make a failing test pass, so it adds Skip = "flaky" to the Fact and reports the suite green
a session marks a test it does not understand as skipped while refactoring, and never returns to it
a session copies a Skip reason from an unrelated test to silence a new failure
classes.gapNotes: Only sees the xUnit Skip form. NUnit's [Ignore("...")] and [Explicit], MSTest's [Ignore], and a test disabled by an environment-gated early return are all invisible to this pattern. It also cannot tell a legitimately skipped platform-specific test from an abandoned one - only the ledger of how long the skip has stood can do that.

evidence.source: xunit.net analyzer rules index (xUnit1004 - Test methods should not be skipped); the rule's own page states SkipWhen/SkipUnless suppress it in v3.

classes.title: Test commented out rather than repaired
agentModes: a session comments out the attribute rather than the whole method, so the code still compiles and the test silently disappears from the run
a session comments out a failing assertion block while 'temporarily narrowing scope' and leaves it
a session wraps a test region in #if false to get a green build
classes.gapNotes: Matches a commented-out xUnit attribute only - '// [Fact]' or '// [Theory]', with the attribute first in the comment. A test disabled by wrapping the method in a /* ... */ block leaves nothing on a '//' line and is not matched, and NUnit's [Test] and MSTest's [TestMethod] spellings are not matched either. It cuts the other way too: a comment that quotes '[Fact]' while explaining something is flagged, so this class needs a wave-off path. S125 is the wider net for the shapes the pattern does not reach, but it is a general commented-out-code rule rather than a test-aware one - it fires on any commented block that parses as code, so an explanatory comment carrying a snippet is a false positive there as well, and it cannot tell a commented-out test from commented-out production code. Neither detector sees an '#if false' region, which disables a test with no comment marker at all. A test method deleted outright leaves no trace in the file for either to find - that needs a test-count comparison against the previous commit or a coverage baseline.

evidence.source: SonarSource rule csharpsquid:S125 'Sections of code should not be commented out' (sonar-dotnet); confirmed against next.sonarqube.com's rule index. Confidence is heuristic because SonarSource's own tracker (sonar-dotnet issue 3659) documents that S125's line-ends-in-semicolon-or-brace heuristic produces false positives.

classes.title: Assertion softened to a tautology
agentModes: a session replaces Assert.Equal(expected, actual) with Assert.True(true) after failing to reproduce the expected value
a session downgrades a value assertion to Assert.NotNull or Assert.True(true) so the test passes without proving anything
a session leaves a placeholder assertion behind after 'stubbing out' a test it planned to finish
classes.gapNotes: Catches only the literal tautology. The commoner softening - swapping Assert.Equal for Assert.NotNull, loosening an exact decimal to a range, or asserting on a value the code under test just returned - is semantically identical to a legitimate assertion and cannot be told apart by a regex or by any rule id in this ecosystem. xUnit2020 covers always-FAILING boolean asserts, not always-passing ones, so it is deliberately not claimed here.

evidence.source: Checked the full xunit.analyzers rules index for an always-passing-assertion rule; xUnit2020 is 'Do not use always-failing boolean assertion to fail a test', which does not cover this, so no tool-rule detector is claimed.

classes.title: Test that asserts nothing
agentModes: a session writes a test that exercises the path and stops, so the test passes as long as nothing throws
a session deletes the failing assertion and leaves the arrange/act body in place
a session generates a scaffold of test method names to satisfy a coverage request and never fills the bodies in
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector: counting assertions requires walking a method body, and any regex approximating it would flag every test whose assertions live in a shared helper. S2699 has the same blind spot - SonarSource documents that it does no cross-file analysis, so a test whose assertions sit in a custom helper class is a false positive unless the helper's methods are named with an 'Assert' prefix. Also does not fire on a test that asserts only on its own test double.

evidence.source: SonarSource sonar-dotnet rule S2699 'Tests should include assertions' (RSPEC-108/RSPEC-2699 family); the cross-file limitation is stated in the rule's own description.

classes.title: Empty catch block
agentModes: a session cannot diagnose a thrown exception, so it wraps the call in try/catch with an empty body and calls the bug fixed
a session adds an empty catch to make an integration test stop failing
a session catches and drops during a refactor because the new signature no longer allows the exception to propagate
classes.gapNotes: Only an empty block counts. A catch whose body is a single log call, a return of a default value, or a bare 'return;' swallows the failure just as completely and is invisible to both the pattern and S108. The pattern depends on comments being stripped first, so a catch containing only an explanatory comment reads as empty and is flagged - intended here, but it is also the one place this class and S108 disagree: S108 explicitly exempts a block that contains a comment, so the pattern fires where the rule stays silent.

evidence.source: SonarSource sonar-dotnet rule S108 'Nested blocks of code should not be left empty' (RSPEC-108); the conditional-compilation false positive is tracked in sonar-dotnet issue 4540.

classes.title: Catching System.Exception
agentModes: a session widens a specific catch to catch (Exception) so an unanticipated failure stops surfacing
a session adds a top-level catch (Exception) around new code it is unsure about
a session converts a caught, typed exception into a logged-and-continue catch-all while 'making the handler more robust'
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic on purpose: a catch-all at a process boundary - a message pump, a hosted service loop, a top-level Main - is legitimate and will be flagged. Those sites need an explicit .editorconfig exclusion or a scoped suppression rather than a rewrite. Catching a broad-but-not-Exception type such as SystemException or a custom base class is not matched by the pattern, though CA1031 does flag SystemException.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn code quality rule CA1031 'Do not catch general exception types'; the rule flags System.Exception and System.SystemException and accepts a rethrow as the last statement.

classes.title: Nullable context switched off in a file
agentModes: a session hits a wall of CS8618/CS8602 warnings in a file it is editing and puts #nullable disable at the top
a session adds #nullable disable to a generated-looking file rather than annotating the members it touched
a session flips <Nullable>disable</Nullable> in the project file to make the build go green
classes.gapNotes: Sees only the source directive. <Nullable>disable</Nullable> in a csproj or Directory.Build.props achieves the same thing project-wide and is covered by a different class; a project that never enabled nullable in the first place produces no directive at all and is invisible here. '#nullable disable warnings' is matched, which is correct, but so is a legitimate disable in a hand-maintained generated file - those need a path exclusion.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn C# reference, nullable reference type warnings: the nullable context is set by the <Nullable> MSBuild property or the #nullable preprocessor directive.

classes.title: Null-forgiving operator used to silence the compiler
agentModes: a session appends ! to a dereference to clear CS8602 rather than adding the null check the warning is asking for
a session initialises a non-nullable field to null! to clear CS8618 in a type it did not want to redesign
a session sprinkles ! through a call chain while migrating a file to nullable-enabled
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic. EF Core models and DI-populated properties legitimately use 'null!' initialisers, and the pattern here does not match those (it only matches x!.Member), so the commonest legitimate use is spared but the commonest abusive one - null! on a field - is missed. IDE0080 only fires when the operator is provably unnecessary, so it is not claimed as a tool rule.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn documents the null-forgiving operator and IDE0080 'Remove unnecessary suppression operator'; IDE0080 does not cover a ! that is genuinely suppressing a real maybe-null state, so the detector is check-driver only.

classes.title: #pragma warning disable never restored
agentModes: a session adds #pragma warning disable at the top of a file to clear a diagnostic and never emits the matching restore
a session disables a rule id it cannot satisfy so the -warnaserror build passes
a session widens the scope of an existing scoped suppression by deleting the restore line
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic, not deterministic: the lookahead only matches a restore of the same rule id later in the same file, so the legal bare form 'disable CS8602 ... #pragma warning restore' with no id - which restores every disabled warning - reads as unrestored and is a false positive on correct code. A multi-id disable ('disable CS8602, CS8604') captures only the first id, so the second is never checked for a restore either. It cannot judge whether a correctly scoped suppression is justified, and says nothing about suppressions moved into .editorconfig as severity = none, which is the quieter version of the same move.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn C# preprocessor directives (#pragma warning) and 'How to suppress code analysis warnings'; IDE0079 is documented but only reports suppressions that are provably unnecessary.

classes.title: SuppressMessage attribute added instead of a fix
agentModes: a session decorates the offending member with [SuppressMessage] rather than satisfying the rule
a session adds an assembly-level suppression to GlobalSuppressions.cs so a whole namespace stops reporting
a session copies a SuppressMessage attribute from another file, including its unrelated Justification text
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic because the pattern does not detect the class it is named for: it flags every SuppressMessage, blanket or not, including ones a reviewer approved with a real justification. This is a review prompt, not a verdict, and needs a wave-off path. It cannot read the Justification text to judge quality. IDE0079 is a real, confirmed rule but is aimed at a different target - it reports a suppression that suppresses nothing, not a suppression that is too broad - so a well-formed blanket suppression of a rule that IS firing passes IDE0079 cleanly. Neither detector sees the equivalent move made in .editorconfig (dotnet_diagnostic.CAxxxx.severity = none), which is the same suppression with no attribute to find.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn 'How to suppress code analysis warnings' (SuppressMessageAttribute, GlobalSuppressions.cs) and code-style rule IDE0079 'Remove unnecessary suppression'.

classes.title: NoWarn widened to bury a real diagnostic
agentModes: a session appends the failing rule id to <NoWarn> in Directory.Build.props so -warnaserror stops failing
a session adds 'nullable' to NoWarn to clear a whole class of warnings at once
a session adds a CA or xUnit id to NoWarn while 'unblocking the build' and does not mention it in the summary

fixtures.violation:
<Project>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CS8602;CA1031</NoWarn>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="SonarAnalyzer.CSharp" PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
fixtures.nearMiss:
<Project>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CS1591;NU5104</NoWarn>
    <WarningsNotAsErrors>NU1701</WarningsNotAsErrors>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="SonarAnalyzer.CSharp" PrivateAssets="all" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

classes.gapNotes: Only sees ids matching the shapes listed, so a numeric-only entry (<NoWarn>8602</NoWarn>, which the compiler accepts) slips through, as does <WarningsNotAsErrors>. The near-miss shows the legitimate case this must not break: CS1591 (missing XML doc) and NU5104 are routinely and correctly suppressed. It also cannot tell a suppression added today from one that predates the repository's guardrails. MSBuild files are read without an XML comment rule, so a <NoWarn> parked inside an <!-- --> comment counts as live and is reported even though the build never reads it.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn C# compiler options - errors and warnings: NoWarn accepts warning numbers with or without the CS prefix and the literal 'nullable'; WarningsNotAsErrors overrides TreatWarningsAsErrors.

classes.title: TreatWarningsAsErrors turned off
agentModes: a session flips TreatWarningsAsErrors to false so a build with outstanding warnings succeeds
a session sets CodeAnalysisTreatWarningsAsErrors to false so only the CA rules stop failing, which reads as a smaller change
a session lowers WarningLevel while 'reducing build noise'

fixtures.violation:
<Project>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>false</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <CodeAnalysisTreatWarningsAsErrors>false</CodeAnalysisTreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>false</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
fixtures.nearMiss:
<Project>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
    <NuGetAudit>true</NuGetAudit>
    <NuGetAuditMode>all</NuGetAuditMode>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>false</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <ProduceReferenceAssembly>false</ProduceReferenceAssembly>
    <IsPackable>false</IsPackable>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

classes.gapNotes: Requires the closing angle bracket immediately after the element name, so a conditioned form - <TreatWarningsAsErrors Condition="'$(CI)' != 'true'">false</TreatWarningsAsErrors> - is not matched, and that conditioned form is exactly how a session hides the change from a local build. It also cannot see the property being unset entirely, or -warnaserror being dropped from the CI command line, which has the same effect. MSBuild files are read without an XML comment rule, so a <TreatWarningsAsErrors>false</TreatWarningsAsErrors> left inside an <!-- --> comment is reported as if it were in force.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn C# compiler options - errors and warnings (TreatWarningsAsErrors), code analysis overview (CodeAnalysisTreatWarningsAsErrors, EnforceCodeStyleInBuild) and NuGet auditing packages (NuGetAudit).

classes.title: API, package or namespace that does not exist
agentModes: a session writes a using directive for a namespace it has confused with one from another library version
a session calls a method that sounds right - ToFrozenList, JsonSerializer.DeserializeStrict - and never verifies it exists
a session adds a PackageReference to a package id it invented, or to a version that was never published
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector: a regex cannot know which namespaces and members exist. The violation fixture deliberately does not compile - the compile failure IS the signal, which means this class is only enforceable by actually building, not by inspecting a diff. It also does not cover an invented NuGet package id; that surfaces as NU1101 at restore time, which the nuget-audit toolchain entry's restore step will catch but which is not claimed as a rule here.

evidence.source: C# compiler errors CS0246 (type or namespace name could not be found) and CS1061 (type does not contain a definition for a member); both are standard Roslyn diagnostics emitted by dotnet build.

classes.title: dynamic used to get past the type checker
agentModes: a session changes a parameter or return type to dynamic when it cannot work out the right type
a session uses dynamic to bridge two shapes it did not want to model, moving the failure to runtime
a session widens a generic constraint to dynamic while 'making the helper reusable'
classes.gapNotes: Covers only 'dynamic' as a declared type. The quieter widening moves - changing a parameter from a concrete type to object, replacing a generic constraint with a base class, or swapping a record for a Dictionary<string, object> - are all legal, idiomatic-looking C# with no rule id behind them, and this class does not see any of them. 'dynamic' in a legitimate COM or ExpandoObject interop file will be flagged and needs a path exclusion.

evidence.source: Searched the CA and IDE rule indexes for a rule discouraging 'dynamic'; none exists, so this is check-driver only and marked heuristic.

classes.title: Credential or connection string in source
agentModes: a session inlines a placeholder API key to make a sample run and leaves it in the committed file
a session pastes a connection string from a log or a config dump directly into a class
a session hardcodes a token in a test fixture because it could not wire up the configuration provider
classes.gapNotes: Must run with stripStrings off, which makes it one of the two classes in this edition that read literal text - so it will also fire on obviously fake sample values in documentation-style files. Matching is case-sensitive on the common casings only, because JS RegExp has no inline (?i) flag and the check driver passes no flags: a SCREAMING_SNAKE or lowercase spelling outside the listed forms is missed. A base64 or hex secret assigned to a neutrally named constant (var k = "aGVsbG8...") matches nothing here. There is no CA rule for hardcoded credentials, so no tool-rule detector is claimed; a dedicated secret scanner in CI is the real answer and this class only narrows the window.

evidence.source: Reviewed the CA security rule index (CA2100, CA5350/CA5351, CA5394); none of them covers a credential literal, so this class is check-driver only.

classes.title: Endpoint or path hardcoded instead of configured
agentModes: a session inlines the production base address into a client rather than binding it from IConfiguration
a session hardcodes an absolute file path from its own working directory
a session pins a URL it saw in a log so the code will 'work now', bypassing the options pattern already in the project
classes.gapNotes: Narrow by design: only a literal URL wrapped in 'new Uri(...)' is matched, so an address passed straight to HttpClient.GetAsync, an absolute filesystem path, a port number, or a magic timeout is missed entirely. Test projects and options-class defaults legitimately hold literal URLs, as the near-miss shows - its default survives only because it is not wrapped in new Uri - so this needs a paths exclusion for tests and for *Options.cs or it will be noisy enough to be waved off. No analyzer rule in this ecosystem reports a hardcoded endpoint, so nothing backstops the shapes the pattern misses.

evidence.source: No CA or IDE rule exists for hardcoded endpoints; the .NET options pattern (IOptions<T>, IConfiguration) is the documented alternative this class points at.

classes.title: Test run narrowed by a filter
agentModes: a session adds a TestCaseFilter that excludes the category its change broke
a session appends --filter to the CI test step so a subset runs and the job goes green
a session moves a failing test into a category and then excludes that category in .runsettings

fixtures.violation:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<RunSettings>
  <RunConfiguration>
    <ResultsDirectory>./TestResults</ResultsDirectory>
    <TreatNoTestsAsError>true</TreatNoTestsAsError>
    <TestCaseFilter>(TestCategory != Flaky) & (TestCategory != Integration)</TestCaseFilter>
  </RunConfiguration>
  <LoggerRunSettings>
    <Loggers>
      <Logger friendlyName="trx" enabled="True" />
    </Loggers>
  </LoggerRunSettings>
</RunSettings>
fixtures.nearMiss:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<RunSettings>
  <RunConfiguration>
    <ResultsDirectory>./TestResults</ResultsDirectory>
    <TreatNoTestsAsError>true</TreatNoTestsAsError>
    <TestSessionTimeout>600000</TestSessionTimeout>
    <MaxCpuCount>0</MaxCpuCount>
  </RunConfiguration>
  <TestRunParameters>
    <Parameter name="webAppUrl" value="http://localhost:5001" />
  </TestRunParameters>
  <LoggerRunSettings>
    <Loggers>
      <Logger friendlyName="trx" enabled="True">
        <Configuration>
          <LogFileName>results.trx</LogFileName>
        </Configuration>
      </Logger>
      <Logger friendlyName="blame" enabled="True" />
    </Loggers>
  </LoggerRunSettings>

classes.gapNotes: Only sees an exclusionary filter committed to a runsettings or project file. The same narrowing done as --filter on the CI command line lives in a workflow YAML, which is not C# and is not in this class's paths - a separate CI-file class or a diff check on the test step is needed for that. An inclusive filter that quietly omits a suite (TestCategory = Unit only) is also missed, since it contains no != operator. Runsettings and MSBuild files are read without an XML comment rule, so a <TestCaseFilter> parked inside an <!-- --> comment is reported even though vstest never applies it.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn 'Configure unit tests with a .runsettings file' (RunConfiguration/TestCaseFilter) and dotnet test with VSTest (--filter operators =, !=, ~, !~).

classes.title: A run that discovers no tests still exits zero
agentModes: a session reports the suite green when the run actually discovered zero tests - a broken adapter reference, a wrong project path, an over-narrow filter
a session sets TreatNoTestsAsError to false after a discovery failure rather than fixing discovery
a session drops the test project from the solution and the CI step keeps exiting zero

fixtures.nearMiss:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<RunSettings>
  <RunConfiguration>
    <ResultsDirectory>./TestResults</ResultsDirectory>
    <TreatNoTestsAsError>true</TreatNoTestsAsError>
    <TreatTestAdapterErrorsAsWarnings>false</TreatTestAdapterErrorsAsWarnings>
    <TestSessionTimeout>600000</TestSessionTimeout>
  </RunConfiguration>
  <LoggerRunSettings>
    <Loggers>
      <Logger friendlyName="trx" enabled="True">
        <Configuration>
          <LogFileName>results.trx</LogFileName>
        </Configuration>
      </Logger>
    </Loggers>
  </LoggerRunSettings>

classes.gapNotes: Catches the setting being flipped, not the underlying condition. A repository with no .runsettings at all inherits the default of false and is silently exposed - the absence of a file cannot be detected by a pattern over files, so jig must assert the file exists as a separate install-time check. It also says nothing about a test project that was dropped from the solution, where discovery legitimately finds nothing to run. Runsettings and MSBuild files are read without an XML comment rule, so a <TreatNoTestsAsError>false</TreatNoTestsAsError> sitting inside an <!-- --> comment is reported as if it were in force, while the opposite move - commenting out a working <TreatNoTestsAsError>true</TreatNoTestsAsError> - leaves nothing for the pattern to match and passes silently.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn 'Configure unit tests with a .runsettings file' - TreatNoTestsAsError defaults to false; dotnet test with VSTest exit codes section states a run that discovers no tests returns 0 by default.

classes.title: Async result blocked on synchronously
agentModes: a session calls .Result or .Wait() to avoid propagating async up a call chain it did not want to change
a session uses GetAwaiter().GetResult() inside a test to avoid making the test method async
a session blocks in a constructor or property getter because the signature cannot be made async
classes.gapNotes: Deliberately omits '.Result' from the pattern: a property named Result is common on result-object records, and matching it produces false positives faster than jig can wave them off - the near-miss carries one to prove the point. That means the single commonest form of this mistake is caught only by CA1849 (inside an async method) and xUnit1031 (inside a test), not by the check driver. Blocking in a constructor of a non-async class is caught by neither rule.

evidence.source: xunit.net analyzer rule xUnit1031 'Do not use blocking task operations in test method'; Microsoft Learn code quality rule CA1849 'Call async methods when in an async method'.

classes.title: async void method
agentModes: a session writes async void so a call site that expects void will compile, and the exception is now unobservable
a session converts a sync handler to async and leaves the return type as void
a session writes an async void test method, which xUnit v3 no longer runs
classes.gapNotes: Flags every async void, including the one legitimate case - a UI or classic event handler whose signature the framework fixes - so WinForms, WPF and MAUI code-behind files need a path exclusion. xUnit1049 only covers test methods, so async void in production code has no tool rule behind it in this edition and rests on the pattern alone.

evidence.source: xunit.net analyzer rules xUnit1048 (async void deprecated in v3) and xUnit1049 (async void no longer supported for test methods).

classes.title: Task started and never awaited
agentModes: a session calls an async method as a bare statement, so the work is fire-and-forget and its exception is lost
a session removes an await while making a method synchronous and leaves the call in place
a session drops an await inside a loop to 'parallelise', without collecting the tasks
classes.gapNotes: Leans on the Async naming convention, so a task-returning method not suffixed with Async is invisible, and a non-task-returning method that happens to end in Async is a false positive. It also cannot see a call whose arguments span several lines, since it runs per line. CS4014 is the real backstop and is far more precise, but it is a warning - it only fails the build with TreatWarningsAsErrors on, which is why the csc toolchain entry sets it.

evidence.source: C# compiler warning CS4014 ('Because this call is not awaited, execution of the current method continues before the call is completed'); the CS-prefixed warning is promoted to an error by TreatWarningsAsErrors.

classes.title: System.Random used for a security value
agentModes: a session generates a token, nonce or reset code with new Random() because it is the first API that comes to mind
a session replaces a cryptographic generator with Random while 'simplifying' a helper
a session seeds Random with a constant to make a test deterministic and leaves that helper in production code
classes.gapNotes: The pattern flags every new Random(), including entirely legitimate non-security uses - jitter, shuffling a demo list, seeding a fixture - so it is heuristic and will need waving off in those files. It does not match Random.Shared, which is the modern form and equally unsuitable for secrets; CA5394 does cover Random.Shared and is the more accurate detector of the two.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn code quality rule CA5394 'Do not use insecure randomness'; System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator.GetInt32 is the documented replacement.

classes.title: Broken or weak cryptographic algorithm
agentModes: a session reaches for MD5 or SHA1 to hash a value because those are the examples it has seen most often
a session matches an existing legacy MD5 call when adding a new code path, spreading the algorithm
a session picks MD5 for a 'checksum' that is in fact a security boundary
classes.gapNotes: Only matches the static factory and one-shot forms. An instance created through CryptoConfig.CreateFromName("MD5"), an algorithm name held in configuration, or a HashAlgorithmName.MD5 value passed to a KDF all evade the pattern - CA5350 and CA5351 catch most of those and are the reason both are wired here. Neither rule nor pattern can tell a genuine non-security checksum (cache key, ETag) from a security use, so waved-off sites need an .editorconfig scope.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn code quality rules CA5350 'Do Not Use Weak Cryptographic Algorithms' (TripleDES, SHA1, RIPEMD160) and CA5351 'Do Not Use Broken Cryptographic Algorithms' (MD5, DES, RC2).

classes.title: SQL built by string interpolation
agentModes: a session interpolates a value straight into a command because parameterising it required touching the calling signature
a session converts a parameterised query into an interpolated one while 'simplifying' a repository method
a session builds a dynamic WHERE clause by concatenation to satisfy a filtering requirement
classes.gapNotes: Catches interpolation at the command boundary only. Concatenation with + into a local that is later assigned to CommandText, a query assembled by a StringBuilder, or raw SQL passed to Dapper or EF Core's FromSqlRaw are all missed by the pattern - CA2100 covers the IDbCommand.CommandText path but not the ORM helpers. The near-miss carries an interpolated log message on purpose: that is the shape a looser pattern would wrongly flag.

evidence.source: Microsoft Learn code quality rule CA2100 'Review SQL queries for security vulnerabilities'; the rule targets IDbCommand.CommandText built from string arguments.
